planting.note: Surface-sow seed after the last frost in lean, fast-draining soil in full sun and do not cover, since portulaca seed needs light to germinate; Sun Frost was an early All-America Selections winner prized for its cream-white leaf margins as much as its flowers.

directions: Sun Frost is an All-America Selections-winning moss rose distinguished from other Portulaca grandiflora cultivars by its variegated foliage, with narrow, needle-like succulent leaves edged in a soft cream-white band that gives the whole mound a frosted look even before the flowers open. Bright red-orange, rose-like blooms appear over the frosted foliage all summer and, unlike many older seed-strain portulacas, hold up reasonably well into overcast afternoons. Grow it in lean, gritty, well-drained soil in full sun, since rich soil and excess moisture encourage lanky growth and root rot. The low, spreading mound is well suited to rock gardens, gravel beds, hot dry parking strips, and the edges of raised beds where its variegated foliage adds interest even between flushes of bloom. Let the soil dry out between waterings and avoid fertilizing heavily, which produces soft, disease-prone growth at the expense of flowering.

common_name: Kingwood Gold Jewels of Opar (Golden-Leaved Fameflower)

planting.note: Set out nursery starts or rooted cuttings after the last frost into well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Kingwood Gold holds its bright chartreuse-gold color best with some afternoon shade in hot climates and reseeds true to color less reliably than the green species, so division or cuttings are the surest way to maintain the exact clone.

directions: Kingwood Gold is a golden-foliage selection of jewels of opar, grown for its glowing chartreuse-yellow succulent leaves rather than for its small pink flowers alone, though the same airy, widely branched sprays of tiny rosy-pink blooms still rise above the foliage through summer and into fall. The bright color makes it a favorite foliage accent for combining with dark-leaved companions in mixed borders and containers, where it lights up shaded corners that would otherwise call for pale flowers. Plant in average to lean, well-drained soil; too much shade fades the gold color toward green, while too much hot afternoon sun in dry soil can scorch the leaves, so morning sun with afternoon shade is the reliable sweet spot in warm climates. It tolerates heat and drought once established and self-seeds in favorable conditions, though seedlings often revert partly toward green and named-color plants are best renewed from cuttings or divisions. Treat as an annual outside its hardiness range or overwinter cuttings indoors on a bright windowsill.
sources: North Carolina State University Cooperative Extension

common_name: Variegated Heartleaf Ice Plant (Variegated Baby Sun Rose)

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or divisions after the last frost into well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade; this variegated form is slower and less vigorous than the plain green species, and stems that revert to solid green should be cut out to keep the variegation strong.

directions: This variegated selection of heartleaf ice plant carries the same small, glossy, heart-shaped succulent foliage as the species but edged and splashed in creamy white, giving trailing mats a bright, two-toned look even before the small magenta-pink daisy flowers open in sun. It roots readily from stem cuttings pressed into well-drained soil and spreads as a low, trailing groundcover, container spiller, or hanging basket subject, tolerating a bit more shade and regular moisture than most true ice plants. Because it is a sport of the green species, occasional shoots will revert to solid green; pinch these out promptly so they do not outcompete and eventually overtake the variegated growth. Being frost-tender, grow it as a summer annual or overwinter cuttings indoors in a bright spot outside its hardiness range, and pinch leggy stems to keep plantings dense and colorful.

common_name: Red Apple Ice Plant (Vigorous Heartleaf Ice Plant)

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or divisions after the last frost into well-drained, average soil in full sun; Red Apple is a larger-growing, more vigorous selection than the species and roots easily from stem sections that touch the soil.

directions: Red Apple is a robust selection of heartleaf ice plant grown widely as a fast, tough bank and slope cover, especially in coastal and Mediterranean-climate landscapes, with larger, glossier succulent leaves and more prolific, deeper red-orange flowers than the species. Its trailing stems root wherever a node touches soil, letting a planting fill in quickly to control erosion on slopes or spill over walls and raised beds. It is more drought-tolerant than the plain species once established, needing only occasional deep watering, and full sun brings on the heaviest flowering. Cut back hard in spring to remove any winter dieback or bare woody centers and to encourage dense new growth, and take cuttings for easy propagation or for overwintering indoors where winters bring hard frost.
sources: University of California Marin Master Gardeners

planting.note: Separate offsets from established rosettes and pot in fast-draining, gritty cactus mix; grow in bright light with some protection from the harshest midday sun, which can bleach or brown the pearled leaf surface.

directions: Pearl plant forms an upright, spiraling rosette of thick, dark green, incurving leaves whose surfaces are entirely covered in raised, pearly white tubercles, giving the whole plant a beaded, sugared appearance quite distinct from the banded stripes of zebra-type haworthias. It is a slow-growing South African succulent that prefers bright light with some shade from intense afternoon sun, since strong direct exposure can bronze or scorch the tubercled leaf surface, while too little light causes the rosette to stretch and lose its compact form. Plant in a very fast-draining, mineral-heavy succulent or cactus mix and allow the soil to dry completely between waterings, cutting back watering further in winter. It offsets steadily at the base to form a slowly spreading clump, and offsets can be removed and potted separately once they have their own roots. Grow outdoors year-round only in essentially frost-free, dry climates; elsewhere it is best suited to a bright windowsill or protected patio as a houseplant.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America
